# Diagnosing Multi-Cylinder Misfires on a Jeep Liberty 3.7L V6

When you encounter a misfire affecting cylinders 1, 3, and 5 on a 2003 Jeep Liberty equipped with the 3.7-liter V6, the pattern immediately signals a specific hardware architecture issue rather than random component failure. These three cylinders share a common trait: they are all located on the driver's side of the engine block. In this configuration, the ignition coils are mounted on top of the intake manifold and fire in pairs. The coil assembly for cylinder 1 is paired with cylinder 4, the coil for cylinder 3 pairs with cylinder 6, and the coil for cylinder 5 pairs with cylinder 2.

Because cylinders 1, 3, and 5 are firing simultaneously but are grouped on one side of the engine, a single point of failure affecting all three is highly improbable if the root cause were simply the internal resistance of the coils themselves. If you have already swapped individual coil packs or inspected the connectors and found no damage, shifting your diagnostic focus to the power delivery system is the logical next step.

### The Power Distribution Bottleneck

The most probable culprit for a simultaneous misfire across cylinders on one bank is a failure in the main ignition power feed. On this specific engine platform, the primary power source feeding the driver-side coil packs often originates from a single fuse or a specific circuit branch that splits to supply all three coils. If that upstream connectionâwhether it is a blown fuse, a corroded relay contact, or a fractured wire within the harnessâis compromised, every coil on that side will lose voltage simultaneously.

You can verify this without immediately disassembling the engine bay by checking the voltage at the main power input terminal for the driver-side ignition circuit. Use a multimeter to measure voltage relative to ground while the engine is cranking or running. If the voltage drops significantly below 12V or fluctuates wildly, you have identified a supply issue rather than a coil failure.

### Shortcutting the Power Check

To implement a shortcut for checking power delivery effectively, locate the main connector harness that feeds the three coils on the driver's side. You do not need to remove the coils to perform this check. Instead, back-probe the main power pin (often labeled as the "hot" or battery feed) at the harness connector itself with the engine running.

If you have access to an oscilloscope or a high-quality logic analyzer, capturing the waveform will reveal if the signal is clean or if there is significant noise indicative of a failing ignition control module or driver-side PCM (Powertrain Control Module). However, for most service scenarios, a simple DC voltage measurement with a multimeter set to 20V range is sufficient.

If you measure full battery voltage at the harness connector but the coils still fail to fire, the issue likely lies in the ground path shared by these components or within the internal driver circuitry of the PCM that controls the coil triggers. Conversely, if you measure low voltage, your investigation should move to the fuse box under the hood or in the cabin, looking for a dedicated fuse often labeled "IGNITION" or similar, depending on the specific year's wiring diagram variations.

### Common Pitfalls and Misdiagnoses

A frequent error when troubleshooting this pattern is assuming that because the coils are failing, they must be replaced individually. While coil packs do fail, it is statistically unlikely for three coils on the same side to fail internally at the exact same time without an external cause. Replacing them one by one will only lead to wasted labor and parts costs if the root electrical supply issue remains unresolved.

Another consideration is the condition of the ignition control module (ICM). On some iterations of this engine, the ICM is integrated into the PCM. If the driver-side circuit within the PCM has failed, it can cut power to all coils on that side simultaneously. Before condemning the entire PCM, ensure there are no obvious signs of physical damage to the connector or harness, such as melted insulation or corroded pins, which often result from heat exposure near the exhaust manifold.

Resolving this misfire requires methodical verification of the electrical supply chain rather than component replacement alone. By confirming that power is reaching the driver-side coil cluster, you can avoid unnecessary part swaps and address the actual root cause of the ignition failure.
